data.title: Banco de Chile Delivers Strong Earnings Amid Caution
data.description:
Banco De Chile ((BCH)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Summer Sale - Claim 70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Banco de Chile’s latest earnings call painted a largely upbeat picture, with management emphasizing strong revenue momentum, leading margins, and robust profitability despite a cooling Chilean economy. Executives balanced optimism with prudence, pointing to higher inflation volatility, added provisions, and slightly softer growth and ROE targets, but stressed that capital and liquidity leave the bank well placed for a rebound.

Strong Operating Revenue Growth

Operating revenues surged to CLP 922 billion in the second quarter, a 20.9% year‑on‑year increase, supported by higher inflation and healthy loan and fee expansion. Management stressed that this growth is not one‑off, noting broad‑based contributions across client segments and products, which helps cushion macro softness.

Superior Margin and Net Financial Income

Net financial income climbed 25.3% year‑on‑year to CLP 736 billion, confirming Banco de Chile’s margin leadership in its market. The bank reported a net interest margin of about 4.9% in the first half and an operating margin of 6.8%, far above industry averages and underpinned by its strong deposit mix and disciplined pricing.

Robust Profitability

Net income reached CLP 391 billion in the quarter, translating into an impressive quarterly ROE of roughly 27.9%. Year to date, ROA stood at 2.4% and ROE at about 22.9%, with management highlighting recurring income and active balance sheet management as key drivers rather than isolated trading gains.

Industry‑Leading Efficiency

The bank’s cost discipline continued to stand out, with the efficiency ratio improving to 31.3% in the quarter and 34.5% for the first half. Operating expenses rose only 2.8% year‑on‑year, well below inflation, while loans per employee increased to CLP 3.6 billion, showcasing productivity gains and operating leverage.

Resilient Fee and Customer Income

Fee income remained a bright spot, growing 10.7% year‑on‑year, powered by a 20.4% jump in transactional fees and a fee margin of 1.4% over interest‑earning assets. The bank now serves about 2.9 million active customers and boasts an NPS score of 77.6, which management cited as evidence of strong franchise quality and cross‑sell potential.

Deposit Franchise and Funding Strength

Banco de Chile reinforced its position as a funding powerhouse with a 19.7% market share in local currency demand deposits. These deposits make up roughly 26% of funding and the demand‑deposits‑to‑loans ratio is 36%, the highest among peers, providing a structural advantage on funding costs and margin resilience.

High Capital and Coverage Levels

Capital metrics remained comfortably above regulatory minima, with a Basel III ratio of 17.6% and CET1 at 13.9%. Loan loss allowances covered 127% of past‑due loans, and nearly 230% including additional allowances, giving the bank a sizable buffer to absorb potential credit losses in a slower economy.

Commercial and Digital Momentum

Total loans reached CLP 40.3 trillion, up 2.3% year‑on‑year, or 2.9% when adjusted for a card migration effect that reduced reported balances by about CLP 210 billion. Consumer originations rose 8% and SME installment lending grew 18% versus the first half of 2025, while digital current accounts jumped 34% and overall current account openings increased 17%.

Strategic Partnerships and Product Innovation

Management highlighted several new initiatives, including the launch of B Startup and alliances with partners such as UDD Ventures and AWS to support entrepreneurs and tech‑driven clients. Additional partnerships with Linze, Despegar and Fingo are designed to deepen presence in auto finance, travel loyalty and SME factoring, opening new fee and lending avenues.

Macroeconomic Slowdown and Revised Growth Forecast

The macro backdrop in Chile remained a headwind, with GDP slipping around 0.2% year‑on‑year in the first half and Q2 growth barely positive. In response to persistent supply‑side shocks, notably in mining, Banco de Chile cut its 2026 GDP forecast to 1.3%, signaling a more subdued operating environment for loan demand.

Higher Inflation and Policy Uncertainty

Inflation has re‑accelerated, rising from 2.4% in February to 4.3% in June, and the bank now expects roughly 4% inflation for the full year alongside a policy rate near 4.5%. Management warned that oil prices and geopolitical tension could keep inflation and rates more volatile, affecting both asset pricing and funding conditions.

Additional Provisions Increased Cost of Risk

The bank booked CLP 50 billion of additional provisions in May, lifting the quarterly cost of risk to 1.65%, or about 1.15% excluding the extra buffer. Executives said this conservative stance, which shaved roughly 90 basis points off ROA and ROE guidance, is meant to front‑load credit protection amid macro uncertainty.

Conservative Guidance and Lower Loan Growth Outlook

Reflecting the weaker backdrop, Banco de Chile trimmed its 2026 nominal loan growth outlook to about 6% from 7% and now guides for a year‑end NIM of roughly 4.6%. The bank framed this as prudence rather than a shift in strategy, emphasizing that its high spreads and funding strength should allow it to outperform industry margins.

Rising Consumer Delinquency

Consumer loan delinquency ticked up from 1.8% to 2.1% year‑on‑year, although the overall non‑performing loan ratio stayed low at 1.6%. Management acknowledged some deterioration in consumer credit against a weaker employment backdrop, but argued that strong coverage and early provisioning mitigate the associated risk.

Tax Reform One‑Time and Transitional Impacts

Executives outlined the impact of Chile’s tax reform, noting a recurring long‑term benefit from a lower corporate rate estimated at about CLP 40 billion per year. However, they cautioned that the change will also bring a sizable one‑time negative income tax effect and create some temporary uncertainty around deferred tax calculations.

One‑Time Operational Reclassification Effecting Comparability

The migration of outsourced credit card processing prompted a change in how some balances are recorded, causing a one‑off reduction of around CLP 210 billion in reported credit card loans and certain demand deposits. Management stressed that this is purely an accounting reclassification and complicates year‑on‑year comparisons rather than underlying performance.

External Risks and Industry Headwinds

Beyond domestic challenges, the bank flagged geopolitical conflicts, El Niño weather patterns and slower growth in China as key external risks. These factors could keep inflation and market volatility elevated and weigh on loan demand and margins across the Chilean banking industry, even as Banco de Chile expects to maintain an edge.

Forward‑Looking Guidance and Outlook

Updated guidance assumes nominal loan growth of about 6%, a year‑end NIM near 4.6% and a cost of risk between 1.2% and 1.3%, above earlier expectations as additional provisions are factored in. The bank targets an efficiency ratio improving toward 37% by late 2026 and a return on average capital and reserves of 21% to 22%, supported by strong capital ratios and a long‑term dividend payout near 60%.

Banco de Chile’s earnings call showcased a bank firing on most cylinders, with strong revenues, high margins, and excellent efficiency offsetting a tougher macro tide and higher risk costs. For investors, the message was one of disciplined growth and conservative provisioning, suggesting the franchise is built to ride out volatility while remaining well positioned for an eventual recovery in Chilean credit demand.

data.title: Mirum Pharmaceuticals Earnings Call Highlights Growth Momentum
data.description:
Mirum Pharmaceuticals ((MIRM)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Summer Sale - Claim 70% Off TipRanks

  • Unlock powerful investing tools with TipRanks Premium to make smarter, more confident investment decisions
  • Subscribe to TipRanks Smart Investor Newsletter, and discover new investing opportunities with data-backed stock picks

Mirum Pharmaceuticals’ latest earnings call struck an upbeat tone, underscored by strong revenue growth, expanding margins and a reinforced balance sheet. Management highlighted a rich slate of upcoming clinical and regulatory milestones that could further transform the business, while acknowledging that new regulatory hurdles in PSC introduce meaningful uncertainty that investors will need to monitor closely.

Strong Quarterly Revenue Growth

Mirum reported Q2 2026 net product sales of $176.0M, up from $128.0M a year earlier for a 37.5% YoY increase. Executives credited broad portfolio demand and effective commercial execution, signaling that the company’s rare‑disease franchise is gaining traction across both established and newer treatment markets.

Raised Full-Year Sales Guidance

On the back of the robust quarter, Mirum lifted its 2026 net product sales guidance to a range of $680M–$700M. The higher outlook reflects confidence in sustained demand for existing medicines and the company’s ability to maintain growth momentum as its therapies penetrate global markets.

Livmarli and Bile Acid Portfolio Strength

Livmarli remains Mirum’s commercial engine, generating $129M in Q2 sales, with $92M from the U.S. and $37M from international markets. Bile acid medicines added roughly $48M, helped by increased adult PFIC diagnosis and expanding reimbursement abroad, supporting management’s case for Livmarli’s long‑term blockbuster potential.

Balance Sheet Reinforced by Convertible Notes

Mirum closed the quarter with $561M in cash, cash equivalents and investments, up from $391M at the start of the year. The company issued $690M of 0% convertible notes, netting $672M, and used part of the proceeds to settle 75% of its 2029 notes, adding $197M in cash and reducing future interest expense while posting positive operating cash flow.

Commercial Margin Expansion

The commercial cash contribution margin reached the high‑50s percent in the first half of 2026, an improvement of about 5 percentage points versus the prior year. Management framed this margin expansion as evidence that scaling the rare‑disease portfolio is beginning to deliver stronger profitability, even as the company continues to invest heavily in growth initiatives.

Pipeline Momentum and Near-Term Catalysts

Investors heard a detailed update on Mirum’s pipeline, with several catalysts approaching. Zilurgisertib faces a September PDUFA and could launch in the U.S. in Q4, while EU filings are already submitted, and volovitug’s AZURE‑1 and AZURE‑4 readouts this year may support a potential BLA in H1 2027 alongside EXPAND and MRN‑338 data.

Regulatory Recognition for Volixibat in PSC

The company emphasized that VISTAS, testing volixibat in PSC‑related cholestatic pruritus, met its primary endpoint and won Breakthrough Therapy designation from regulators. That status reflects recognition of volixibat’s potential to address a significant unmet need for PSC patients suffering from severe itching, an area with limited current options.

Phase 3 Requirement Delays PSC Timeline

Despite the positive data, Mirum disclosed that a pre‑NDA meeting led regulators to recommend a Phase 3 study for volixibat in PSC. As a result, the company has pushed its planned NDA submission back to the first half of 2027, introducing added execution risk and delaying expected PSC commercialization compared with earlier plans.

Uncertainty Around PSC NDA Package

Management stressed that VISTAS delivered statistically and clinically persuasive results but admitted they are not yet aligned with regulators on what constitutes an acceptable NDA package. This lack of clarity could require further data or extended dialogue and leaves the PSC pathway as a key overhang amid otherwise strong corporate momentum.

Elevated Operating Expenses and R&D Investment

Q2 operating expenses totaled $290M, including $16M of in‑process R&D tied to the Zilurgisertib license and $76M of R&D, with $29M devoted to volovitug. SG&A reached $66M, cost of sales $23M and noncash items such as stock‑based compensation and amortization added $37M, reflecting Mirum’s willingness to spend aggressively to build and diversify its pipeline.

PSC Revenue Timing Pushed Out

The revised regulatory path for volixibat means potential PSC revenue will arrive later than previously envisioned. While core products continue to grow, investors should factor in that PSC‑related contributions are now unlikely to materialize before 2027, increasing near‑term uncertainty around that particular indication.

Forward-Looking Guidance and Outlook

Looking ahead, Mirum’s raised 2026 sales guidance and strong cash position underpin a confident outlook, even as expenses remain high. The company is preparing for a possible Q4 launch of Zilurgisertib, multiple key readouts for volovitug, EXPAND and VANTAGE into 2027, and early proof‑of‑concept data for MRN‑338, setting up a catalyst‑rich period for shareholders.

Mirum’s earnings call painted a picture of a company balancing strong commercial performance with ambitious clinical goals, tempered by regulatory friction in PSC. For investors, the story remains one of solid growth, rising margins and a deep pipeline, with the main watch point centered on how effectively management navigates the PSC setback and converts upcoming milestones into durable revenue.
